issues.legal_issue: An admitted copy of an authority to sell, when the original is withheld by the party who possesses it, can establish the agent’s authority without further formal proof.
material_facts: The owner admitted that his brother was his registered power of attorney holder, but claimed the authority was limited to managing the property.
The buyer produced a copy of the registered power of attorney; the owner admitted the signature and contents when shown the document.

The owner did not produce the original, which was in the defendants’ possession, and correspondence also showed that the owner had authorized his brother to negotiate a sale and receive consideration.
The registered power of attorney authorized the brother to sell the property, collect the proceeds and execute the necessary documents.
issues.conclusion: The power of attorney did not require further proof under Sections 65 and 66 of the Evidence Act once its signature and contents were admitted. The evidence established the agent’s authority to sell, and the High Court erred in finding otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: Where a party admits the signature and contents of a document produced in copy, further proof under Sections 65 and 66 of the Evidence Act is unnecessary. When the opposing party withholds the original document in its possession, the court should not disregard the admitted copy and related evidence. No earlier case is cited for this determination.

rule.if: specific_performance_appeal and authority_document_copy_produced and document_signature_and_contents_admitted and original_withheld_by_opposing_party and document_authorizes_sale

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a claim for specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.authority_document_copy_produced: A party produced a copy of a document purporting to authorize an agent to deal with the property.
predicates.document_signature_and_contents_admitted: The opposing party admitted the signature and contents of the authority document.
predicates.original_withheld_by_opposing_party: The original authority document was in the opposing party’s possession but was not produced by that party.
predicates.document_authorizes_sale: The authority document empowers the agent to sell the property and complete the sale.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance appeal involves an admitted copy of sale authority and the opposing party withholds the original, the agent’s authority to sell is established if the document authorizes the sale.

issues.legal_issue: A rise in property value during litigation, by itself, does not justify refusing specific performance, though the court may impose reasonable conditions to balance the parties’ equities.
material_facts: A registered sale agreement was executed through an agent authorized to sell the owner’s share of the property.
The trial court found that the buyer had paid the consideration and had remained ready and willing to perform, while the defendants had not completed the sale.
The buyer filed suit relatively soon after the agreement, but the dispute remained in court for many years and the property’s value increased substantially.
The Supreme Court restored the decree for specific performance on condition that the buyer pay an additional amount to the owner.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s refusal of specific performance was set aside. The trial court’s decree was affirmed subject to a reasonable additional payment condition to account for the circumstances, including the substantial increase in value during the prolonged litigation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the discretion to grant specific performance must be exercised judicially on fair and reasonable principles. A rise in price or passage of time alone is not a valid reason to deny relief, although the court may impose a reasonable condition, including additional payment, after considering the totality of the circumstances. The Court relied on Satya Jain v. Anis Ahmed Rushdie, Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd., V. Pechimuthu v. Gowrammal and K. Prakash v. B.R. Sampath Kumar; it distinguished K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan and Vimaleshwar Nagappa Shetty v. Noor Ahmed Sheriff on their facts.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and valid_sale_agreement_proved and buyer_continuously_ready_willing and seller_failed_to_complete_sale and property_value_increased_during_litigation

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.valid_sale_agreement_proved: The sale agreement is legally valid and proved.
predicates.buyer_continuously_ready_willing: The buyer remained ready and willing to perform the buyer’s obligations under the agreement.
predicates.seller_failed_to_complete_sale: The seller failed to complete the sale as agreed.
predicates.property_value_increased_during_litigati: The property increased in value while the dispute was being litigated.

issues.definition: If a proved sale agreement, the buyer’s continuing readiness and willingness, the seller’s failure to complete the sale, and an increase in value during litigation are present in a specific-performance suit, the court may grant specific performance subject to reasonable conditions.

issues.legal_issue: A party who misrepresents material facts and withholds material evidence cannot rely on equitable discretion to defeat specific performance.
material_facts: The defendants claimed that the agent’s authority was limited to managing the property, although the registered authority empowered him to sell it.
The defendants did not produce the original authority document despite possessing it.
The defendants denied the sale agreement despite the registered agreement and evidence that the agent had received consideration under it.
issues.conclusion: The defendants’ conduct disentitled them from seeking the exercise of discretion against specific performance; the Court also recognized its inherent power to prevent abuse of the process of law.
issues.legal_principle: The discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 is equitable and must be exercised on sound judicial principles. A party that fails to disclose material facts truthfully, misleads the court or suppresses material evidence should not obtain a discretionary refusal of relief on equitable grounds. The Court invoked the principles stated in Rooke’s Case and Attorney General v. Wheat concerning judicial discretion, and its inherent power to prevent abuse of process.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.seller_misrepresented_material_facts: The seller gave the court a materially false account of the transaction or the agent’s authority.
predicates.seller_withheld_material_evidence: The seller withheld material evidence in the seller’s possession from the court.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, a seller who misrepresents material facts and withholds material evidence cannot obtain refusal of specific performance in the seller’s favor on equitable grounds.
